summary: RFC 7432 provides Designated Forwarder election for multihomed Ethernet Segments, enhanced by the Highest Random Weight algorithm. This document improves these procedures by providing a faster recovery after failures.

plainLanguage.summary: When the helper in charge of a job drops out, another must take over. This makes the swap happen faster.

questions: how to speed up df election
what is evpn designated forwarder election
how does evpn fast df recovery work
subtitle: Lets EVPN routers hand over Designated Forwarder duties at an agreed clock time, so recovery is fast without loops or long drops.

tldr.problem: When a failed or new provider edge router joins a multihomed Ethernet Segment, the timer-based DF election in RFC 7432 either risks duplicate traffic and loops (timer too short) or prolonged traffic loss (timer too long).
tldr.mechanism: The recovering router advertises a Service Carving Time in a new BGP extended community, and all peers perform the DF election at that clock-synchronized moment, with a small skew so the old forwarder stops just before the new one starts.
tldr.outcome: The 3-second timer window shrinks to the order of milliseconds. If any peer does not signal support, everyone falls back to the RFC 7432 timer behavior. It updates RFC 8584.

today: RFC 9722 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2025. It updates RFC 8584, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The DF Election Recovery Problem
sections.content:
In EVPN (RFC 7432), a customer site can be multihomed to several provider edge (PE) routers. For each VLAN, one PE is the Designated Forwarder (DF) and the others are Non-Designated Forwarders (NDF) that block traffic. RFC 8584 added the Highest Random Weight (HRW) algorithm so a failure does not needlessly reshuffle VLANs.

This document adds an option for fast DF election when a failed link or node recovers. It is independent of the number of EVPN Instances on the Ethernet Segment and works through simple one-way BGP signaling between the recovered node and its peers. It updates the DF election state machine of RFC 8584 by optionally adding delays between some events.
sections.plainLanguage: When a helper comes back from a break, the group has to decide who does which job again, and this RFC makes that decision quick and safe.

sections.title: Why Timers Fall Short
sections.content:
Several PEs encapsulate and decapsulate traffic for the same VLAN. A moment when two of them both act as DF can cause duplicated frames, Layer 2 loops and broadcast storms. Split-horizon filtering can prevent loops but not duplicates, and with overlapping DFs the check can fail.

HRW cannot help when a PE is inserted or a port is newly added, because the DF role has to move to the new port while the old DF is still active. In the RFC's example (CE1 multihomed to PE1 and PE2), there is no handshake between PE1 and PE2 when PE2 recovers.

RFC 7432 and RFC 8584 use a timer to synchronize the transfer. A timer that is too short causes loops and duplicates. A timer that is too long causes prolonged traffic loss. The RFC 7432 approach favors drops over duplicates, so each PE recovery involves drops for as long as the timer (default 3 seconds).
sections.plainLanguage: If the hand-over waits too little, two guards stand in the road. If it waits too long, nobody guards it.

sections.title: Synchronizing on a Service Carving Time
sections.content:
All PEs on an Ethernet Segment have synchronized clocks (for example with NTP or PTP). When a PE is inserted or recovers, it sends its peers the current time plus its partner discovery timer from step 2 of Section 8.5 of RFC 7432. This absolute time is the Service Carving Time (SCT), carried in a new BGP EVPN Extended Community alongside the Ethernet Segment route (Route Type 4).

Peers perform the DF election at that time. To avoid overlap they use a skew, with a default of 10 ms. Previously inserted PEs perform DF to NDF transitions first (at SCT minus skew) and NDF to DF transitions at the SCT. The recovering PE already has every service in NDF state, so it needs no skew and acts when its own timer expires. Implementations may use a larger or configurable skew, depending on scale, hardware and clock accuracy.

Where possible, recovery of a failed PE SHOULD NOT start until the clock synchronization protocol has converged. If clocks are badly out of sync, the timestamp range checks keep convergence no worse than RFC 7432.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone looks at the same clock. The helper coming back says 'we swap at exactly this time', and the helper on duty steps away a hair before.

sections.title: BGP Encoding and the Time Synchronization Capability
sections.content:
The SCT is an extended community with Type 0x06 and Sub-Type 0x0F. It holds a 32-bit Timestamp Seconds field (NTP seconds, epoch 0 h 1 January 1900 UTC) and a 16-bit Timestamp Fraction field holding the high-order 16 bits of the NTP fraction. A receiver rebuilding a 64-bit NTP timestamp sets the lower 16 bits to zero. The precision is 15 microseconds (2^-16 s).

A new Time Synchronization capability, bit 3 (the T bit, corresponding to bit 27 of the DF Election Extended Community from RFC 8584), signals the wish to use this procedure. It works together with the agreed DF election type, such as HRW. A PE that does not support the procedure, or sees a route without the capability set, MUST NOT delay DF election, because that could cause overlapping DFs.
sections.plainLanguage: The agreed time is written as a small time stamp attached to a message, plus a checkbox that says 'I can do this clock trick'.

sections.title: Timestamp Checks and the Updated State Machine
sections.content:
The NTP Era value is not exchanged, so PEs treat timestamps as being in their own Era. The next Era transition falls on February 7, 2036. A PE that receives an SCT smaller than its current time MUST discard it and treat the DF election at the peer as already done, which falls back on RFC 7432 behavior. Implementations MUST also check the received SCT against an upper bound. The recommended bound is the local peering timer: an SCT whose offset is larger MUST be discarded in the same way.

The update to RFC 8584 changes action 9 for the transition from DF_CALC to DF_DONE. After an Ethernet Segment route arrives with an SCT, the PE waits until the SCT minus skew, assumes the NDF role, waits the remaining skew, and only then takes the elected role (DF or NDF). Without an SCT it proceeds immediately. The states and events are unchanged, only the timing.
sections.plainLanguage: A router ignores a time that has already passed or one that is absurdly far away, and just uses the old safe method instead.

sections.title: Worked Scenarios
sections.content:
With the old procedure and the default 3-second timer, PE2 recovers at t=99 and advertises RT-4 at t=100. PE1 carves immediately, so some VLANs go NDF at once. PE2 only carves at t=103, so traffic drops for that whole window.

With the SCT, PE2 advertises RT-4 at t=100 with an SCT of t=103. PE1 starts a service carving timer for t=103 and both carve at t=103, PE1 slightly earlier for DF to NDF changes. The BGP propagation delay no longer matters, and the 3-second window shrinks to the order of milliseconds. The RFC says this encourages larger peering timer values.

If two or more PEs recover at about the same time, each advertises an SCT, and all PEs execute a single DF election at the latest received SCT. In the RFC's example, PE2 advertises t=103, then PE3 recovers at t=102 and advertises t=105, so PE1, PE2 and PE3 all carve at t=105. If a recovering PE does not support or advertise the T bit, all PEs in the current sequence immediately revert to RFC 7432 behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: If two helpers return at nearly the same time, everyone waits for the later agreed time and does one big swap.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
PEs using the baseline modulo-based algorithm from RFC 7432 simply discard the unrecognized SCT extended community. If one or more PEs on the Ethernet Segment do not signal T=1, all PEs SHALL revert to the timer-based approach of RFC 7432, which helps prevent VLAN shuffling with more than two PEs. If an RT-4 arrives without the T capability during an ongoing election, all SCT-based delays are cancelled and the election applies immediately.

The security considerations of RFC 7432 and RFC 8365 apply. For the new community, attacks could set the value to zero, to a past time or to a time far in the future, and these are handled by the timestamp verification rules above. IANA assigned Sub-Type 0x0F (Service Carving Time) and bit 3 (Time Synchronization) in the relevant registries.
sections.plainLanguage: If even one router does not know the clock trick, everybody goes back to the old method so nothing goes wrong.
